title: Constrained Subsequence Sum
description: Find the maximum sum subsequence where consecutive picks are at most k apart, using DP accelerated by a monotonic decreasing deque.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the maximum sum of a non-empty subsequence such that for every two consecutive chosen elements at original indices i and j (i < j), j - i <= k. In other words, any gap between two chosen elements can be at most k - 1 unchosen elements.

blocks.caption: A monotonic deque finds the best usable previous dp value within the last k positions in O(1) amortized.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (can contain negatives), k (maximum index gap between consecutive chosen elements)"],["Constraint","A chosen subsequence must have consecutive picks at most k indices apart"],["Goal","Maximize the sum of the chosen elements"],["Note","The subsequence must be non-empty, so even an all-negative array has a valid answer (the single largest element)"]]}

blocks.text: This is structurally identical to Jump Game VI: define dp[i] as the best subsequence sum ending exactly at index i, where dp[i] depends on the maximum dp value among the last k positions. The only difference is that here, starting fresh at i (ignoring all previous elements) is always allowed, since the subsequence does not have to start at index 0.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Whenever a recurrence needs "the maximum of the last k dp values," reach for a monotonic decreasing deque, exactly the Sliding Window Maximum technique.

Picture a hiker along a trail collecting bonus points at each marker, but any two consecutive collected bonuses must be within k markers of each other. Some bonuses are negative bad markers. The hiker wants to choose which markers to stop at to maximize total points, and can always choose to simply start over from any point if everything collected so far would only drag the total down.

blocks.caption: A fresh start beats carrying forward a negative running total.

items: dp[i] represents the best achievable subsequence sum that ends by definitely including index i.
dp[i] = nums[i] + max(0, best dp value among indices i-k through i-1); the max with 0 represents the option to start the subsequence fresh at i.
The final answer is the maximum dp[i] over all i, since the best subsequence can end anywhere.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The maximum dp value is 37, achieved at i=4 by the subsequence [10, 2, 5, 20] (indices 0,1,3,4, each consecutive gap at most k=2), matching the expected output.
A direct DP recurrence computes dp[i] by scanning back up to k previous dp values to find the best one to extend from. This is correct but re-scans overlapping windows repeatedly.

Since the window slides forward by one each step and only the MAXIMUM matters, a monotonic decreasing deque maintains exactly the useful candidates: indices still within the last k positions, kept in decreasing order of their dp value, so the front of the deque is always the best usable predecessor. This is precisely the Sliding Window Maximum technique applied inside a DP recurrence.
For each index i, scan the previous k dp values directly to find the best one to extend from, taking max(0, that best value) to allow starting fresh.

codes.python:
def constrained_subset_sum(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    dp = [0] * n
    dp[0] = nums[0]
    best = dp[0]

    for i in range(1, n):
        best_prev = 0
        for j in range(max(0, i - k), i):
            best_prev = max(best_prev, dp[j])
        dp[i] = nums[i] + max(0, best_prev)
        best = max(best, dp[i])

    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(constrained_subset_sum([10, 2, -10, 5, 20], 2))
    print(constrained_subset_sum([-1, -2, -3], 1))

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: When k is large (up to 10^5), rescanning the same window repeatedly as it slides forward by one each step is wasted work, since most of the window is shared between consecutive steps.

Maintain a monotonic decreasing deque of indices whose dp values are in decreasing order. Before computing dp[i], evict indices that have fallen outside the k-window from the front. The front of the deque is then the best usable predecessor, giving dp[i] in O(1). After computing dp[i], evict any indices from the back whose dp value is dominated (less than or equal to dp[i]), since they can never be the best choice again while i remains in range, then push i.

items: Evict stale indices (outside the k-window) from the front before reading the best value.
Compute dp[i] = nums[i] + max(0, dp value at the deque's front).
Evict dominated indices from the back, then push i, keeping the deque decreasing.

codes.python:
from collections import deque


def constrained_subset_sum(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    dp = [0] * n
    dq = deque()
    best = float('-inf')

    for i in range(n):
        while dq and dq[0] < i - k:
            dq.popleft()
        best_prev = max(0, dp[dq[0]]) if dq else 0
        dp[i] = nums[i] + best_prev
        best = max(best, dp[i])
        while dq and dp[dq[-1]] <= dp[i]:
            dq.pop()
        dq.append(i)

    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(constrained_subset_sum([10, 2, -10, 5, 20], 2))
    print(constrained_subset_sum([-1, -2, -3], 1))

items: A DP recurrence needing "the max of the last k dp values" is a monotonic-deque sliding-window-maximum problem in disguise.
Allowing max(0, ...) in a DP transition encodes "starting fresh is always an option," letting negative runs be discarded.
This exact deque-accelerated DP pattern reapplies whenever a bounded lookback window feeds into a running optimum.

blocks.text: Constrained Subsequence Sum is solved with dp[i] = nums[i] + max(0, best dp value within the last k indices), accelerated from O(n*k) to O(n) by tracking that windowed maximum with a monotonic decreasing deque, the same technique used in Sliding Window Maximum and Jump Game VI.
